---
title: "Core Setup"
subtitle: "The five steps everyone needs"
---

Work through these in order. At the end you will have a working `rdp-work`
command. Nothing on this page trades away security — the convenience shortcuts
live in [Tips & Hacks](hacks.qmd).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Written and tested on **Ubuntu 24.04 LTS**, both native and under **WSL2**
(where the GUI arrives via WSLg). Any Debian-family distribution should work.
:::

---

## Step 1 — Install the prerequisites {#step-1}

```bash
# Only if a previous apt run was interrupted:
sudo dpkg --configure -a

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y freerdp2-x11 libsecret-tools gnome-keyring
```

That gives you three things: `xfreerdp` (the client), `secret-tool` (the
keyring command-line interface), and the keyring daemon itself.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Ubuntu 25.04 or newer? Use FreeRDP 3

FreeRDP 2 is retired in newer releases. Install version 3 instead:

```bash
sudo apt install -y freerdp3-x11 libsecret-tools gnome-keyring
```

The binary is called `xfreerdp3` rather than `xfreerdp`. Every flag used in this
guide works identically in both versions — you only need to change the command
name. On Ubuntu 24.04 both packages are available; version 2 is the safer default.
:::

Check it landed:

```bash
xfreerdp --version    # or: xfreerdp3 --version
secret-tool --help >/dev/null && echo "secret-tool OK"
```

---

## Step 2 — Create the shared folder {#step-2}

This one folder is the entire file-transfer mechanism. Anything you drop in it
on Linux shows up instantly inside the Windows session, and vice versa.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/rdp_share
```

---

## Step 3 — Store your password in the keyring {#step-3}

Never put your Windows password in `~/.bashrc`. Store it encrypted instead:

```bash
secret-tool store --label="ULMS RDP Password" rdp <ULMS_SERVER_IP>
```

`secret-tool` prompts for the password on stdin and prints nothing back — that
is expected. The `rdp <ULMS_SERVER_IP>` pair at the end is just a lookup key;
it must match exactly when you read the password back later.

Verify it round-trips:

```bash
secret-tool lookup rdp <ULMS_SERVER_IP>
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## If you are on WSL2, do this first

WSL2 has no desktop session, so the keyring daemon is not running and
`secret-tool` fails with **"Cannot autolaunch D-Bus without X11 $DISPLAY"** or
hangs. Start a session bus and unlock the keyring once per terminal:

```bash
eval "$(dbus-launch --sh-syntax)"
echo -n "your-linux-login-password" | gnome-keyring-daemon --unlock --replace --daemonize
```

See [Tips & Hacks → Make the keyring survive WSL2](hacks.qmd#wsl-keyring) for
how to make that automatic instead of typing it every time.
:::

---

## Step 4 — Create your `config.env` {#step-4}

Keeping the host and username in one file means no personal or internal detail
ever gets committed, and the launcher works unchanged for everyone.

```bash
cp config.env.example config.env
```

Then edit `config.env`:

```bash
# The ULMS Windows server address (ask ULMS IT if you do not have it)
RDP_HOST=10.x.x.x

# Your Windows account name
RDP_USER=your_windows_username

# Optional AD domain — leave blank if you sign in with a bare username
RDP_DOMAIN=

# Local folder shared into the Windows session
RDP_SHARE_DIR=$HOME/rdp_share

# The name it appears under in Windows: \\tsclient\<RDP_SHARE_NAME>
RDP_SHARE_NAME=share

# Binary name: xfreerdp (FreeRDP 2) or xfreerdp3 (FreeRDP 3)
RDP_BIN=xfreerdp
```

Lock it down and confirm `.gitignore` is already excluding it:

```bash
chmod 600 config.env
git check-ignore -v config.env    # should print a .gitignore match
```

::: {.callout-important}
`config.env` holds no password — the password stays in the keyring. It is
git-ignored anyway because the server address is internal information.
:::

---

## Step 5 — Wire up the `rdp-work` command {#step-5}

Two routes to the same result. The script is easier to update and share; the
alias is the one-liner from the original write-up.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Launcher script (recommended)

`scripts/rdp-work.sh` in this repository reads `config.env`, pulls the password
out of the keyring, and launches FreeRDP. Make it executable and point a
shell function at it:

```bash
chmod +x scripts/rdp-work.sh
echo "alias rdp-work='$PWD/scripts/rdp-work.sh'" >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
```

The script fails loudly with a useful message if the VPN is down, the keyring
entry is missing, or `config.env` has not been filled in — which is most of the
value over a bare alias.

### Plain alias

Open `~/.bashrc`:

```bash
vim ~/.bashrc
```

Press `G` to jump to the end, then `o` to open a new line in insert mode. Paste
in the following, substituting your own username and server address:

```bash
alias rdp-work='xfreerdp /v:<ULMS_SERVER_IP> /u:<WINDOWS_USER> \
  /p:"$(secret-tool lookup rdp <ULMS_SERVER_IP>)" \
  /dynamic-resolution +clipboard /cert:ignore \
  /drive:share,$HOME/rdp_share'
```

Press `Esc`, then `:wq` to save and quit. Reload your shell:

```bash
source ~/.bashrc
```

:::

### What each flag does

| Flag | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/v:` | The server to connect to. |
| `/u:` `/p:` | Username, and the password read out of the keyring at launch time. |
| `/dynamic-resolution` | The Windows desktop resizes as you resize the window. |
| `+clipboard` | Copy and paste text between Linux and Windows. |
| `/cert:ignore` | Accept the server's self-signed certificate without a prompt. See the note below. |
| `/drive:share,$HOME/rdp_share` | Mounts your local folder as `\\tsclient\share`. |

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## A word on `/cert:ignore`

This disables certificate verification, which in principle exposes you to a
machine-in-the-middle attack. It is here because internal servers typically use
self-signed certificates that would otherwise prompt on every launch. On a
trusted university network behind a VPN the practical risk is low, but it *is* a
real trade-off rather than a free convenience.

The stricter alternative is to connect once without the flag, inspect the
fingerprint, and accept it permanently — FreeRDP stores it in
`~/.config/freerdp/known_hosts2` and stays quiet afterwards while still
detecting a changed certificate.
:::

---

## Using it day to day {#usage}

### Connect

Bring up your VPN if you are off campus, then:

```bash
rdp-work
```

### Move files

- **On Linux:** `~/rdp_share`
- **In Windows:** open File Explorer (`Win`+`E`) → **This PC** → under *Network
  Locations*, **share on tsclient**. Or type `\\tsclient\share` into the address bar.

Files appear on the other side immediately — there is no sync step.

::: {.callout-tip}
Pin `\\tsclient\share` to Quick Access in Windows Explorer on your first session.
The redirected drive is mounted fresh each time you connect, but the pin persists.
:::

### Disconnect

Closing the window suspends the session, leaving your programs running for next
time. To sign out properly, use **Start → your account icon → Sign out** inside
Windows.
